title.en: The Birth and the Wet-Nurse of Muhammad
title.zh: 穆罕默德的誕生與乳母

region.en: Mecca and the desert camp of Banu Sa'd (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 麥加與薩德部族的沙漠營地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, The Life of Mahomet (1877); Ockley, History of the Saracens (Bohn ed. 1890)

source.work: Simon Ockley, The History of the Saracens (Bohn ed.), Life of Mohammed; Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1890; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: Muhammad is born in the Year of the Elephant; his father Abd Allah is already dead, and by the custom of the town his new-born sons are given to the desert. The wet-nurse Halima of Banu Sa'd takes him; his foster-brothers report that two men in white came, opened his breast, took out a black drop and washed his heart in snow; the child returns to his mother, the orphan of Mecca. His grandfather Abd al-Muttalib dotes on him; then, at eight, his uncle Abu Talib takes him in.
summary.zh: 穆罕默德生於象年；其父阿布杜拉已歿。依城中風俗，新生子交沙漠部落乳養；薩德部族乳母哈里瑪收之。其乳兄弟言：二白衣人剖其胸，取出一黑點，以雪洗其心。孤兒歸母；祖父阿布杜·穆塔利卜溺愛之；八歲時叔父阿布·塔里卜收養。

sensitivity.note: Biographical tradition of a living religion; treated as sacred narrative within the tradition. The chest-opening is a cardinal sira miracle; Ockley's rendering reflects early-eighteenth-century English style; paraphrased.

passages.text: In the Year of the Elephant — the year the Lord destroyed Abraha's host with birds throwing baked-clay stones — a son was born to Amina, wife of Abd Allah, who had already died on a trading journey. The child was named Muhammad, 'the praised one'; his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib carried him into the Kaaba, thanked God, and named him as God had chosen. By the custom of the Meccans the new-born were sent out to be nursed in the pure air of the desert, and so the boy passed his first years with the bedouin of Banu Sa'd.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir, Life of Mahomet, 1877; Ockley, 1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: His foster-mother Halima told that while he was with her the blessing of God followed the household: the sheep gave abundant milk and the barren year turned rich. Then his foster-brother came running: 'Two men in white have taken my brother of the Quraysh, thrown him down, opened his breast, and searched it.' They ran back and found the child standing pale with terror. He said: 'Two men in white came to me; they opened my belly, and took out a black clot, and threw it away; then they washed my heart with snow until it was clean, and joined it again.' They carried him back to Mecca to his mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: His mother died on the road returning from a visit to her kin at Yathrib, and the boy was taken by his grandfather, who loved him above all his children: he would sit him by his side at the council, and feed him before himself. When Abd al-Muttalib died, at eight years the boy passed to his uncle Abu Talib, who kept him as his own son — and the orphan of Mecca grew up poor, herding sheep for hire with his brethren.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: Bahira the Monk Sees the Seal of Prophecy

region.en: Busra, on the Syrian caravan road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 敘利亞商路上的布斯臘（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: At twelve the boy travels with his uncle Abu Talib on a caravan to Syria. At Busra the monk Bahira, who had never before honoured the caravan, invites all to a feast; he examines the child, questions him, and finds behind his shoulder-blade the 'seal of prophethood'. He warns Abu Talib: take him back to Mecca and guard him against the Jews, for a great future awaits him. The monk's forgotten feast-guest has shared the caravan's food — the mark of a true apostle.
summary.zh: 十二歲的男孩隨叔父阿布·塔里卜隨商險赴敘利亞。於布斯臘，修士白希拉從未款待過此商隊，卻設宴邀請全部；他察看此童，問其種種，見其肩胛下有『聖印』。他囑阿布·塔里卜帶回麥加，防猶太人——大前程將至。修士未嘗招待過的客人均分得商隊的食物——此乃真使徒之兆。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; the Bahira episode is a famous recognition scene; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: When Muhammad was twelve years old, his uncle Abu Talib took him on a journey to Syria for trade. On the road, at Busra, there was a monk named Bahira, learned in Christian lore, who had a copy of a book of knowledge. He had never before honoured the passing caravans; but when this caravan drew near, he prepared a feast for it, and sent to them: 'I have made ready food for you, men of Quraysh — masters and servants, young and old, come all.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: They came and left their merchandise under the trees, and went in to the monk. Bahira looked at them and found nothing to mark them; but he asked whether anyone of the caravan had been left behind. They answered that all had come but a boy, the youngest, who sat with the baggage. He bade them bring him, and looked long at him, and questioned him of his sleep and his affairs and his lineage, and the boy answered well. Then Bahira looked at his back and saw the seal of prophethood between his shoulders — the very mark his book described. He said to Abu Talib: 'Take your nephew back to his country, and guard him carefully against the Jews, for by God, if they see him and know what I know, they will do him evil. A great future awaits this nephew of yours.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: Khadija's Caravan and the Double Porch
title.zh: 哈蒂嘉的商隊與加倍聘禮

region.en: Mecca, house of Khadija bint Khuwaylid (literal pin)
region.zh: 麥加哈蒂嘉宅（實際定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: The noble merchantwoman Khadija, hearing the honest youth called Al-Amin (the trustworthy), hires him to lead her caravan to Basra. Her slave Maysara follows and sees the trading prosper, and reports the two angels shading him from the sun. Khadija sends a proposal; her father is called to the marriage and given wine, and the dowry is doubled. From this marriage the Prophet receives, years later, the revelation that settles the dowry of daughters.
summary.zh: 高貴的女商人哈蒂嘉，聞誠實青年之名（阿敏——誠實者），雇他領商險赴巴士拉。其僕麥薩拉相隨，見貿易興旺，並報二人為其遮陽。哈蒂嘉求婚；其父被召至婚宴並賜酒；聘禮加倍。多年後先知傳降啟示，確定女兒聘禮。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: Among the nobles of Quraysh was a woman of substance, Khadija daughter of Khuwaylid, who was sought in marriage by many. Hearing of the honest youth — the people called him Al-Amin, the Trustworthy — she offered him the charge of her caravan to Basra, promising him a double wage. He took her goods, and her slave Maysara went with him; and they traded in Syria until the goods were doubled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: Maysara told her lady when they returned how a cloud shaded Muhammad from the heat wherever he went, and how he ate little and slept little, and how a tree bowed down to shade him in the road. Khadija sent to propose marriage; and she called her father, who had drunk wine, and gave him wine until he was flushed; and the dowry was fixed. And the Prophet, when years later the verse came down fixing the dowry of daughters, said that he had had his portion in the house of Khadija.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: The Quraysh rebuild the Kaaba after flood damage, and when the Black Stone is to be set in place the clans nearly come to blows: each wants the honour of carrying it. An old arbiter proposes that the next man to enter through the gate decide. It is Muhammad, then in his thirties; they are content. He spreads his mantle, sets the stone in the midst, and has each clan take an edge, and all carry it together; then he places it with his own hand.
summary.zh: 洪水損毀天房後，古萊氏重修之；黑石復位之際，各部族幾欲相鬥：人人欲承載其榮。一老仲裁建議：由下一位自門入者裁定。乃穆罕默德，時年三十餘；眾皆同意。他鋪開大氅，置石於中，令各部族各執一隅，共同抬運；再親手安放。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: The Quraysh resolved to rebuild the Kaaba, which a flood had damaged. When the work was done and the time came to set the Black Stone in its place, dispute arose: each clan claimed the honour of lifting it. They nearly came to blows; the descendants of Abd al-Dar brought a bowl full of blood, and they took oath upon it that they would fight to the death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Abu Umayya, the oldest of them, said: 'Make the first man who enters the gate your arbiter.' They looked, and behold — it was Muhammad. When they saw him they said, 'We are content; this is Al-Amin, we accept him.' They told him of the matter, and he said: 'Bring me a garment.' They brought him one, and he took the Black Stone and laid it in the middle of the cloth, and said: 'Let each clan take hold of one side; then all of you, rise up with it together.' And they carried it to its place, and he set it in position with his own hand. And the Quraysh swore that they would never again harbour this resentment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: Khadija and Waraqah: The First Believer
title.zh: 哈蒂嘉與瓦拉嘎：第一位信士

region.zh: 麥加哈蒂嘉宅（實際定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: Returning from the cave of Hira shaking with fear, Muhammad says: 'Cover me, cover me.' 'What is the matter?' — 'The angel that used to come to Moses has come to me.' Khadija answers: 'God will never disgrace thee; thou keepest thy promises, bearest the burdens, feedest the poor, and protectest the weak.' She wraps him and goes to her cousin Waraqah, an old Christian scribe who has read the Gospels and Hebrew scripture: 'This is the Namus that came to Moses; would that I were young when he is sent.'
summary.zh: 自希拉山洞歸來，穆罕默德戰慄而道：『覆我，覆我。』『何事？』——『昔日臨摩西的天使臨我。』哈蒂嘉答：『主必不使你蒙羞；你守信諾，負重荷，賙濟窮人，扶助弱者。』她裹他，去見其堂兄瓦拉嘎——一位通曉福音與希伯來經典的年邁基督教抄經者：『此乃臨摩西的納木斯；願他受遣時我尚年輕。』

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: He came back to Khadija trembling: 'Cover me, cover me.' She covered him until his fear was past. Then he told her what he had seen: 'The angel that used to come to Moses has come to me.' She said, 'Be of good cheer, for by God He will never bring thee to shame: thou keepest the ties of kinship, bearest the burdens of the weak, givest to the poor, honourest the guest, and helpest against the troubles of justice.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then she went to Waraqah ibn Nawfal, her cousin, a man grown old who had read the Scriptures, and told him. He said: 'Holy, holy! By Him in whose hand is the soul of Waraqah, if thou hast told me the truth, Khadija, there hath come to him the great Namus that came to Moses before, and he is the prophet of this people. Would that I were young, that I might be alive when he is sent forth; would that I might be by his side when they expel him.' She said, 'Will they expel him?' He said, 'Yes; never came a man with that which thou bringest but he was met with hostility; but if I live to that day I will help him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: Bilal on the Burning Stones: 'Ahad, Ahad'
title.zh: 比拉勒在烙石上：「唯一，唯一」

region.en: Mecca marketplace of Abu Jahl's torment (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 麥加阿布·賈希勒刑場（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: The strong young slave Bilal, master of the blacksmiths, is seized by Umayya ibn Khalaf at noon and thrown on the burning sand with a great rock on his chest: 'You will not be released till you die or deny Muhammad and worship al-Lat and al-Uzza.' Bilal answers with the words of Islam only: 'Ahad, ahad' (One, One). The first to be freed by Abu Bakr's gold is Bilal; Abu Bakr buys the tortured slaves of the weak clans — Bilal, the women of Banu Muzayin — and frees them for Islam.
summary.zh: 強健的年輕奴隸比拉勒，正午被烏馬亞·本·哈拉夫抓走，拋於烙沙之上，胸口壓巨石：『不認穆罕默德、拜拉特與烏莎，就不得釋放。』比拉勒惟誦伊斯蘭之言：『唯一，唯一』。第一位被阿布·伯克爾金銀贖出者是比拉勒；阿布·伯克爾購買弱族受刑奴——比拉勒與穆扎因部的女子——釋放之，以奉伊斯蘭。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; torture of early Muslims is part of the received narrative; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: The persecution grew: the weak believers were seized and tortured. Bilal, the black slave of the Banu Jumah, a strong young man, was dragged out into the glare of the burning sand, with a huge rock laid on his chest, and his master cried: 'You shall remain till you die or deny Muhammad and worship al-Lat and al-Uzza.' But Bilal only answered from under the stone: 'Ahad, ahad' — One, One. The tormentors would leave him at nightfall; he was found saying the same words.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: Abu Bakr, passing, saw him and ransomed him with a slave of stronger body for him, and freed him; and he bought and freed the women of Banu Muzayin who were tortured in the same way. He said: 'I meant by this to defend the weak, and I was distressed for their sake.' And Bilal, the first muezzin of Islam, was to outlive his master by many years, and to stand at last on the roof of the Kaaba when Mecca opened its gates.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: The First Migration: Ja'far Before the Negus
title.zh: 首次遷徙：加法爾見尼格斯王

region.en: Abyssinia, court of the Negus at Aksum (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿比西尼亞阿克蘇姆王廷（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: The Quraysh send envoys with gifts to the Negus to have the emigrants returned. Ja'far ibn Abi Talib pleads the case of a people who worshipped idols, ate carrion, and were brought out by a prophet from their midst to the worship of God alone — and who are now accused of forsaking their ancestral religion. The Negus asks for proof; Ja'far recites the opening of Surah Maryam; the Negus weeps till his beard is wet. To the envoys' demand to hear what Jesus is, Ja'far answers that he is the servant of God, His prophet, His spirit, and His word. The Negus refuses to deliver them and returns the gifts.
summary.zh: 古萊氏遣使攜禮見尼格斯王，欲遣返移民。加法爾·本·阿比·塔里卜陳述：一拜偶像、食腐肉之民，由中間出現的先知引導敬拜獨一真主，今被控棄祖教。尼格斯求聽證；加法爾誦《麥爾彥章》開篇；王泣至鬚濕。使者要求聽耶穌是誰；加法爾答：主的僕人、先知、靈、言語。王拒遣返，還禮。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; the Negus episode touches Christian-Muslim relations; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: The Prophet said to his Companions: 'Go to Abyssinia, for there is a king there with whom none is wronged; it is a land of truth — go, till God shall make for you a way out of your distress.' And a company went by sea, among them Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and were well received in the land of the Negus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Quraysh sent Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'a and Amr ibn al-As with gifts to bring the emigrants back. The Negus assembled his bishops; Ja'far said: 'O King, we were a people of idolatry, eating carrion and committing abominations, neglecting kindred and doing evil; then God sent to us a prophet from among us, whose lineage and truth and trustworthiness we knew. He commanded us to worship God alone and to renounce the stones and idols we used to serve; he enjoined on us prayer, truthfulness, chastity, and kindness to kin.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Negus said, 'Recite to me some of what your companion has brought.' Ja'far recited from the beginning of Surah Maryam. The Negus wept until his beard was wet, and his bishops wept till their books were soaked. Then he said: 'Of a truth this and what Jesus brought have come from the same lamp.' And to the envoys, who demanded the men, he answered: 'These people have sought my protection, and I will not deliver them.' And he returned the gifts they had brought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

region.en: Taif, vineyards of the Hijaz highlands (literal pin)
region.zh: 漢志高地塔伊夫葡萄園（實際定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: After the death of Khadija and Abu Talib, the Prophet goes to Taif to seek a hearing from the three chiefs of Thaqif. They answer with contempt — one offers the temple-worship of Lat, another marriage, another exile; the rabble is set upon him with stones, and he departs bleeding. In a vineyard he prays a long prayer of complaint; the angel of the mountains asks if he would have the two hills crush the city; the Prophet answers: 'No — I hope that God will bring forth of their seed those who will worship God alone.'
summary.zh: 哈蒂嘉與阿布·塔里卜死後，先知往塔伊夫求見薩吉夫三位首領。他們輕蔑相待——一位獻廟祭拉特，一位提親事，另一位令其離去；暴民以石擊之，他流血而去。於葡萄園作長祈禱；山之天使問是否要兩山壓城；先知答：『不必——我望主將於其後裔中出現敬拜獨一主者。』

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; the prayer at Taif is a locus classicus of Muslim ethics under persecution; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: After the deaths of Khadija and Abu Talib, the Prophet set out for Taif to seek support from the chiefs of Thaqif. He spoke to them privately, but they answered with scorn: one said, 'If God has truly sent you, why does He not protect you?'; another said, 'I will tear down the covering of the Kaaba if God has sent you'; the third said, 'I will not speak to you at all.' The rabble were set upon him, and he was driven out of the town and pelted with stones until his ankles bled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: He took refuge in a vineyard outside the town and prayed a long prayer: 'O God, to Thee I complain of my weakness, my few means, and my insignificance among men... If Thou art not angry with me, I care not; Thine approval is my aim.' And as he prayed, the angel of the mountains called to him: 'God has heard the speech of your people to you, and has sent me the angel of the mountains, that I may command them as you wish — shall I bring the two mountains together upon them?' But the Prophet said: 'No; I hope that God will bring forth of their seed those who will worship God alone, and will not associate with Him anything.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: The Pledges of Aqaba: Twelve and Seventy
title.zh: 阿克巴之誓：十二人與七十人

region.en: Al-Aqaba, mountain pass near Mina (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 米那附近阿克巴山口（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: Men of Yathrib hear the Prophet at the pilgrimage fairs. At Aqaba a first band of twelve gives the pledge of women: 'not to associate anything with God, not to steal, not to commit adultery, not to kill your children, not to utter slander, and not to disobey in what is right.' The next year seventy men and women come by night: they give the pledge of war to defend the Prophet — 'and your women and children are in Paradise' — and choose twelve deputies. The pledge of the second Aqaba opens the way of the Hijra.
summary.zh: 雅茲里布人在朝覲集市聽先知傳道。阿克巴，首批十二人立女式之誓：『不配主、不偷盜、不通姦、不殺子女、不誣蔑、不違正命。』翌年，夜間七十男女而來：立戰式之誓以護先知——『你們的子女與妻子在樂園』——並選十二代表。第二次阿克巴之誓開啟遷徙之途。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; the two Aqaba pledges are the constitutional moment before the Hijra; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: Men of the Khazraj and Aws heard of the Prophet at the pilgrimage fair and carried the news to Yathrib; God opened their hearts to Islam. In the pilgrimage season of the twelfth year of his mission, twelve men met him at Aqaba and gave the pledge known as the pledge of women: 'not to associate anything with God; not to steal; not to commit adultery; not to kill your children; not to utter slander; and not to disobey the Prophet in what is right.' He said: 'If you fulfil this, Paradise is yours.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next year, seventy men and two women came in secret at night to Aqaba, and the Prophet came with his uncle Abbas. The men and women gathered; Abbas spoke first: 'Muhammad is in his clan's keeping; you ask him to join you. If you can keep him from his enemies, promise it.' They asked what would be their reward if they held to it. He said: 'Paradise.' They stretched forth their hands, and said: 'We pledge ourselves to war in defence of you against all men.' And they said: 'O Prophet of God, we have laid a hand upon you; and we swear that we will protect you as we protect our wives and children.' He said: 'Your women and your children are in Paradise.' And twelve deputies were chosen to lead the people of Yathrib.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: The Hijra: Two in the Cave

region.en: Cave of Thawr, south of Mecca (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 麥加南方紹爾山洞（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: With Abu Bakr the Prophet slips out of Mecca at night and hides in the cave of Thawr. The Quraysh set a price on their heads and searchers come to the very cave mouth. Abu Bakr fears for the Prophet's life; the Prophet says: 'What think you of two, the third of whom is God?' The tradition tells of a dove's nest at the entrance and a spider's web; the pursuers turn back. After three days the two ride north with a guide, and reach Quba outside Yathrib — the first mosque of Islam.
summary.zh: 先知與阿布·伯克爾夜間出麥加，藏於紹爾山洞。古萊氏懸賞捉拿，搜查者至洞口。阿布·伯克爾恐先知有失；先知言：『兩人之中，其三為主，你以為如何？』相傳洞口有鴿巢與蛛網；追者折返。三日後，二人偕嚮導北行，抵雅茲里布郊外的庫巴——伊斯蘭第一座清真寺。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; the Hijra marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: The clans of Quraysh met in council to kill the Prophet, each clan contributing a man so that the blood-money would be spread. God revealed to him their plot; and he went out at night, and took Abu Bakr with him, and they hid in the cave of Thawr. Abu Bakr had given instructions that his two she-camels should be made ready.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Quraysh searched every road; a search-party came to the mouth of the cave itself, and Abu Bakr whispered: 'If one of them looks down at his feet he will see us.' The Prophet said: 'What think you, Abu Bakr, of two men the third of whom is God?' And the searchers turned back. The tradition tells that a dove had nested at the entrance and a spider had spun its web across the mouth of the cave. After three days the two rode north with a guide, and reached Quba, where the Prophet stayed and built the first mosque of Islam; then he entered Yathrib — henceforth Medina — and the era of the Hijra began.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

title.en: The Charter of Medina and the Turning of the Qibla
title.zh: 麥地那盟約與朝向之改

region.en: Medina, market of the city (literal pin)
region.zh: 麥地那城市場（實際定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: The Prophet writes a charter between the Muhajirun of Quraysh and the people of Yathrib: one community (umma) to the exclusion of others; mutual defence; the Jews have their religion and the Muslims theirs; blood-money shared; the Prophet to judge in every dispute; no protection given to Quraysh; the killing of a believer requited. At the same season the qibla is turned from Jerusalem to Mecca, and the fast of Ramadan is instituted in place of the fast of Ashura.
summary.zh: 先知書寫雅茲里布古萊氏遷民與當地人之間的盟約：一體之民（烏瑪）；相互防衛；猶太人有其教，穆斯林有其教；血錢共擔；紛爭由先知裁決；不得庇護古萊氏；殺信士者償血。同一季節，朝向由耶路撒冷改向麥加，萊麥丹月之齋取代阿舒拉齋。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; the Charter of Medina is read in modern scholarship as a constitutional document; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: The Prophet wrote a document between the Muhajirun and the Ansar, joining the Jews with them in one community: 'The Jews shall have their religion, and the Muslims their religion; the Muhajirun of Quraysh shall keep to their custom, and shall pay blood-money among themselves and ransom their prisoners... The believers shall not forsake a destitute believer by giving him abundant help against murder or debt. No believer shall take as ally a client of another believer, or the freedman of another believer... God's protection is one; the least of them may grant protection to a stranger on behalf of all. And wherever there is dispute among the people of this document which may cause trouble, it shall be referred to God and to Muhammad, the Messenger of God.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the second year the qibla was turned from Jerusalem towards the Kaaba at Mecca, and the Prophet's face was turned to the sacred mosque; and the month of Ramadan was appointed as the month of fasting in place of the fast of Ashura which had been kept among the Muslims of Medina.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

region.zh: 麥加薩法區（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: Umar, the fierce persecutor, resolves to kill Muhammad, and is told by a passer-by that his own sister and her husband have become Muslims. He goes and hears Surah Ta-Ha being read behind a door; when he enters, his sister confesses. The reading continues, and Umar's soul is moved; he goes to the house where the Prophet was, and is met by Hamza: 'What do you want?' — 'I want to believe.' The Prophet praises God; the strongest persecutor has become the mightiest helper.
summary.zh: 兇猛迫害者歐瑪爾決意殺穆罕默德，途中被告知其妹與妹夫已入教。他前去，隔門聽誦《塔哈章》；入門，其妹認罪。誦經續，歐瑪爾心動；至先知所在之宅，遇哈姆扎：『何事？』——『我要歸信。』先知讚美主；最強的迫害者成了最強的助力。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: Umar ibn al-Khattab, one of the strong men of Quraysh, set out one day with his sword to kill the Prophet. He was met by Nu'aym, who said: 'Where are you going?' He said, 'I am going to kill Muhammad.' Nu'aym said, 'Will you not go back to your own house first? Your sister and her husband are Muslims.' Umar went and heard, behind the closed door, a passage of the Quran which had newly been revealed: 'Ta-Ha. We have not sent down the Quran upon thee to be thy distress...' — Surah Ta-Ha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.

passages.text: He knocked; his sister hid the manuscript, but he had heard some of it. He demanded it; when they said they were Muslims he struck her, and then relented. He said: 'Let me see what you were reading.' His sister said, 'You are unclean, and none but the purified may touch it; wash thyself.' He washed, and read: 'Verily I am God; there is no God but Me: therefore serve Me, and observe prayer in My remembrance.' Umar's soul was moved, and he went to the house where the Prophet was. At the door Hamza met him: 'What do you want, Umar?' He said, 'I want to believe.' And the Prophet cried 'Allahu akbar' with such joy that those in the house came out; and Umar became the mightiest helper of Islam.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.
